1.title: Orchestrate Data Pipelines
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Orchestrate Data Pipelines. This module covers the task statement: orchestrate data pipelines. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Choose an orchestration service: Step Functions, Amazon M W A A (Apache Airflow), A W S Glue workflows, EventBridge, Lambda. Build pipelines for performance, availability, scalability, resiliency and fault tolerance. Implement and maintain serverless workflows. Send alerts with Amazon S N S (Simple Notification Service) and Amazon S Q S (Simple Queue Service). --.

1.title: Case Check-In: Kestrel Freight Chains Its Steps
1.text: Our running case is Kestrel Freight. Kestrel Freight Chains Its Steps. Every night: load orders, clean them, join with telemetry, refresh the warehouse, then notify the team. A step sometimes fails because the source is slow. Finance wants a human approval before invoices are published. Your job: run the steps in order, with retries, branches and alerts.

1.title: What Orchestration Does
1.text: What Orchestration Does. Orchestration coordinates many steps (jobs, queries, functions, approvals) into one workflow: order, dependencies, branching, parallel work, retries, error handling, state and monitoring. Choreography (events between loosely coupled services) is the alternative: no central coordinator; use EventBridge and S N S or S Q S for it. A D A G (directed acyclic graph) (directed acyclic graph) is a workflow with no loops: tasks and their dependencies.

1.title: What Orchestration Does, continued
1.text: What Orchestration Does, continued. The figure shows this: Choosing an orchestrator: Step Functions for serverless multi-service workflows, Amazon M W A A for Apache Airflow D A G s, Glue workflows for Glue-only chains, and EventBridge for event routing.

1.title: What Orchestration Does, continued
1.text: What Orchestration Does, continued. A W S Step Functions. Pick it when: Serverless, multi-service workflow with retries, branches, parallel and human approval. Remember: State machine in Jason (Amazon States Language) with a visual editor; Standard and Express; two hundred plus services through the A W S S D K (software development kit); pay per transition or execution. Amazon M W A A. Pick it when: You already use Apache Airflow, need Python-coded D A G s, hundreds of operators and community plugins. Remember: Managed Airflow: D A G s, requirements and plugins live in an S three bucket; autoscaling workers; runs in your V P C (Virtual Private Cloud); always-on environment cost.

1.title: What Orchestration Does, continued
1.text: What Orchestration Does, continued. A W S Glue workflows. Pick it when: A chain made only of Glue jobs and crawlers. Remember: Triggers link jobs and crawlers; a start trigger (schedule, on demand or EventBridge event); run properties share state; visual graph. Amazon EventBridge. Pick it when: Route events and schedule things; start other orchestrators. Remember: Event bus (many-to-many), Pipes (point-to-point with filter and enrichment), Scheduler. A W S Lambda. Pick it when: A single small step or glue code. Remember: Do not build long workflows by chaining functions: no state, retries or visibility. Exam tip: "Serverless orchestration across Glue, Athena, Lambda and E M R (Elastic MapReduce) with retry and error handling" to Step Functions. "Migrate existing Airflow D A G s" to Amazon M W A A.

1.title: Workflow types
1.text: Workflow types. Maximum duration. Standard: One year. Express: Five minutes. Execution model. Standard: Exactly once. Express: At least once (asynchronous Express). Use for. Standard: Long-running, auditable E T L (extract, transform, load) and human approvals. Express: High-volume, short event processing. Service patterns. Standard: Request response,.sync, callback. Express: Request response only. Billing. Standard: Per state transition. Express: Per execution, duration and memory. History. Standard: In Step Functions (kept ninety days). Express: CloudWatch Logs only. This fact moves with the A W S pages, so check the current value before you rely on it.

1.title: Service integration patterns
1.text: Service integration patterns. Request Response: call a service and go on at once after the H T T P response. Run a Job (.sync): call a service and wait until the job finishes: A W S Glue, Amazon Athena, Amazon E M R (on E C two (Elastic Compute Cloud), on E K S (Elastic Kubernetes Service), Serverless), A W S Batch, Amazon E C S (Elastic Container Service) or Fargate, Amazon E K S, A W S Glue DataBrew, SageMaker A I (artificial intelligence), CodeBuild, Bedrock and nested Step Functions. Wait for Callback (.waitForTaskToken): pass a task token and pause (up to the one-year limit) until a worker calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure: used for human approval and external systems; add a HeartbeatSeconds timeout so a lost token does not hang the run.

1.title: Service integration patterns, continued
1.text: Service integration patterns, continued. Optimized integrations (Glue, Athena, E M R, Batch, S N S, S Q S, Lambda, DynamoDB and more) and A W S S D K integrations (over two hundred services).

1.title: Flow control and error handling
1.text: Flow control and error handling. State types: Task, Choice (branch), Parallel, Map (loop over items, including Distributed Map for very large item sets in Standard workflows), Wait, Pass, Succeed, Fail. Retry (error names, interval, max attempts, backoff rate, jitter) and Catch (route failures to a fallback state, such as an S N S alert). Timeouts (TimeoutSeconds) and heartbeats stop stuck tasks. Exam tip: "Wait for a Glue job to finish before the next step" to the.sync integration (glue:startJobRun.sync). "Pause until a manager approves" to.waitForTaskToken.

1.title: Amazon MWAA (Managed Apache Airflow)
1.text: Amazon M W A A (Managed Apache Airflow). Apache Airflow is open-source software to author, schedule and monitor workflows as Python code (D A G s). Amazon M W A A runs it without servers to manage: A W S sets up and patches Airflow, scales workers automatically between a minimum and maximum, runs the scheduler and workers in its own V P C and encrypts with K M S (Key Management Service). Deploy: put D A G files (and requirements.txt, plugins) in an S three bucket; the environment picks them up. Access: the Airflow web U I is public or private (V P C endpoint); permissions come from I A M (Identity and Access Management); operators call Glue, E M R, Athena, Redshift, Batch, Lambda, SageMaker A I, S Q S, S N S and S three.

1.title: Amazon MWAA (Managed Apache Airflow), continued
1.text: Amazon M W A A (Managed Apache Airflow), continued. Monitoring: Airflow task and scheduler logs and metrics go to CloudWatch. Scheduling is part of the D A G (schedule interval or cron), so M W A A also covers skill one point one.five. Trade-off: more powerful and portable, but you pay for the environment while it exists and write Python. Model. Step Functions: State machine (Jason), visual. Amazon M W A A: Python D A G s. Operations. Step Functions: Fully serverless, pay per use. Amazon M W A A: Managed environment, always running. Best for. Step Functions: A W S-native workflows, event-driven, human approval. Amazon M W A A: Existing Airflow, rich operators, complex scheduling and backfills. Exam tip: M W A A troubleshooting starts in CloudWatch Logs (scheduler, worker, D A G processing) and the D A G s in S three (Module ten).

1.title: Glue workflows
1.text: Glue workflows. A workflow orchestrates crawlers, jobs and triggers and records the status of each step as a graph. A start trigger is a schedule (cron), on demand, or an EventBridge event (for example an object arriving in S three), optionally batched by event count and a window (default and maximum nine hundred seconds). Triggers inside the workflow fire when previous jobs or crawlers succeed, fail or time out. Run properties are name or value pairs shared between jobs in a run. Keep a workflow to one hundred or fewer jobs, crawlers and triggers. Use blueprints to create common workflows.

1.title: Amazon EventBridge
1.text: Amazon EventBridge. Event bus: many-to-many routing with rules and event patterns; sources include A W S services, SaaS partners and your apps. Pipes: point-to-point from a source (S Q S, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, M S K (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) and more) through optional filter and enrichment to a target (such as Step Functions); you pay only for events that match the filter. Scheduler: time-based starts (Module one). Glue job state changes and many other service events appear on EventBridge, so a rule can send a failure alert or start the next pipeline. Exam tip: "A new file in S three must start a multi-step pipeline" to S three to EventBridge rule to Step Functions (or a Glue workflow).

2.title: Building Reliable, Scalable Pipelines
2.text: Building Reliable, Scalable Pipelines. Performance. Parallel branches and Map iterations; right-sized engines; columnar data; avoid serial steps that could run together. Scalability. Serverless and auto scaling services (Glue, Lambda, Step Functions, on-demand Kinesis); decouple stages with queues and streams. Availability. Managed multi-A Z (Availability Zone) services; no single server; multi-A Z M W A A and D M S (Database Migration Service); cross-Region copies for disaster recovery. Resiliency and fault tolerance. Retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, checkpoints and bookmarks, idempotent steps, timeouts, catch and compensate, partial reruns from the failed step. Operability. Logs, metrics, alarms, correlation I Ds, tags; infrastructure as code for repeatable deployments.

2.title: Building Reliable, Scalable Pipelines, continued
2.text: Building Reliable, Scalable Pipelines, continued. Idempotent means a step can run twice with the same result (overwrite a partition, upsert by key): the basis of safe retries. Dead-letter queue (D L Q): a queue that keeps messages that could not be processed after a set number of tries, for inspection and redrive. Decoupling with S Q S: producers write to a queue; consumers scale on queue depth and absorb bursts. Exam tip: "A downstream service is slow or fails sometimes and the pipeline must not lose data" to put an S Q S queue (with a D L Q (dead-letter queue)) between the stages and make the consumer idempotent.

2.title: Serverless Workflows
2.text: Serverless Workflows. A serverless workflow uses managed, auto-scaling services and no servers to patch: Step Functions (control), Lambda and Glue (compute), EventBridge (events and schedules), S Q S and S N S (messaging), S three, DynamoDB, Athena (data). Implement: define the state machine, grant least-privilege I A M roles per step, set retries, timeouts and catches, add alarms, deploy with IaC (A W S S A M (Serverless Application Model), CloudFormation, C D K (Cloud Development Kit): Module five). Maintain: version and alias Lambda functions; version state machines; watch CloudWatch metrics and logs; review failed executions; keep costs in check (Express for high volume, Standard for long runs). A W S Glue and Athena are serverless; M W A A and E M R on E C two are not.

2.title: Notifications and Alerts: SNS and SQS
2.text: Notifications and Alerts: S N S and S Q S. Model. Amazon S N S: Publish or subscribe (push). Amazon S Q S: Queue (pull). Delivery. Amazon S N S: One message to many subscribers: email, S M S (Short Message Service), mobile push, H T T P, Lambda, S Q S, Firehose. Amazon S Q S: One message to one consumer at a time. Use for. Amazon S N S: Alerts, fan-out. Amazon S Q S: Buffering, decoupling, work queues. Features. Amazon S N S: Message filtering by attributes; F I F O (first in, first out) topics. Amazon S Q S: Standard (at least once, best-effort order) and F I F O (exactly once, ordered); D L Q; visibility timeout; long polling; retention up to fourteen days. Alert pattern: CloudWatch alarm or EventBridge rule (for example a failed Glue job) to S N S topic to email, chat bot, ticketing or Lambda. Fan-out pattern: S N S topic to several S Q S queues, each feeding a different consumer.

2.title: Notifications and Alerts: SNS and SQS, continued
2.text: Notifications and Alerts: S N S and S Q S, continued. Step Functions can publish to S N S or send to S Q S directly (Catch states often do). Exam tip: "Notify the team when a pipeline fails" to EventBridge or CloudWatch alarm to S N S. "Buffer records so consumers can process at their own pace" to S Q S.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Step Functions: Serverless state machine. .sync: Wait for a job (Glue, Athena, E M R, Batch, E C S, );.waitForTaskToken equals callback or human approval plus heartbeat. M W A A: Managed Apache Airflow; D A G s in S three; autoscaling workers; own V P C; logs in CloudWatch; not serverless. Glue workflows: Jobs plus crawlers plus triggers. EventBridge: Bus (many-to-many), Pipes (point-to-point plus filter plus enrich), Scheduler. Reliability: Retries with backoff, D L Q, idempotent steps, checkpoints, timeouts, decoupling with S Q S. Alerts: CloudWatch alarm or EventBridge to S N S; S N S fan-out to S Q S; S Q S retention up to fourteen days.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Kestrel Freight's nightly pipeline must run an A W S Glue job, wait for it to finish, run an Athena query, and send a notification if any step fails. The team wants no servers to manage. Which service should orchestrate it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Step Functions is serverless, integrates with Glue and Athena with the Run a Job pattern, and supports retries and catch states. M W A A is not serverless, and chained Lambda functions lack state and visibility.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A company already has hundreds of Apache Airflow D A G s written in Python. It wants to move them to A W S with the least change. Which service fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Amazon M W A A runs Apache Airflow, so existing D A G s, operators and plugins can be reused, with D A G s stored in S three.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A Step Functions workflow must pause until a manager approves an invoice outside A W S, then continue. Which integration pattern should be used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The callback pattern pauses the task until an external process returns the task token with SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure; add a heartbeat timeout so a lost token does not hang the run.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Select two. A step in a data pipeline sometimes fails because the downstream service is briefly overloaded. The pipeline must not lose records and must tolerate the slow service. Which two design choices help? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and D. A queue decouples the stages and absorbs slowness, a dead-letter queue keeps messages that keep failing, and idempotent consumers make retries safe. The other options remove safeguards.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A pipeline made only of A W S Glue jobs and crawlers must start when a new object arrives in S three and show the status of each step as a graph. What is the simplest option? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Glue workflows orchestrate jobs and crawlers, can be started by an EventBridge event such as an S three object arriving, and display the run as a graph.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which statement about Step Functions Express workflows is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Express workflows run up to five minutes, are built for high-volume short workloads, support only the Request Response pattern, and send history to CloudWatch Logs.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: D. Question two: D. Question three: B. Question four: C and D. Question five: A. Question six: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
